policy.hypotheses: Local proposals only. Confirm a candidate from compatible pre-correction responses; no diagnosis from an answer alone.
policy.assistance: Record help before serving tutoring; preserve the first independent answer, but all later retries on this item stay assisted.
policy.display: Server controls response shuffle and keeps stable authoring IDs distinct from opaque client response IDs.
policy.fallback: Unreviewed/stale metadata uses ordinary authorized explanation. Missing approved transfer means a truthful gap.
policy.strict: No tutor payload during an active Strict Mock.

target.prompt: What amount does the question ask you to find?

options.text: The interest charge alone
options.feedback: Keep the borrowed money separate from the extra charge. Next identify the base amount.

options.text: The borrowed money plus interest
options.feedback: Which quantity were you trying to report when you chose your answer?

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: Interest is the extra borrowing charge. The question asks for that charge alone.

options.text: I thought the question wanted the total repayment
options.feedback: That supports a target-quantity mix-up in this attempt. Calculate the extra interest but do not add the principal to the requested answer.

options.text: I knew it wanted interest, but added the principal anyway
options.feedback: That may be an extra step rather than a misunderstanding of the words. Stop when the interest has been found.

options.text: I do not remember, used another method, or selected by mistake
options.feedback: We do not know the cause yet. Separate principal and interest before calculating.

principal.prompt: In this question, what does {principal} represent?

options.text: The amount originally borrowed
options.feedback: Yes. This is the principal used to calculate simple interest.

options.text: The interest already owed
options.feedback: The wording says this amount was borrowed. It is the principal, not a calculated charge.

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: The principal is the starting loan amount. Here it is {principal}.

rate.prompt: What does {rate}% per year mean here?

options.text: {rate} out of every 100 of the original principal for each full year
options.feedback: Yes. Under this simple-interest model the base stays the original principal.

options.text: {rate}% of a new balance that includes earlier interest each year
options.feedback: Which base did you use for later years?

options.text: Exactly ₱{rate} for the whole loan each year
options.feedback: Did you treat the rate numeral as a fixed peso charge?

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: Percent means out of 100. The annual charge is that fraction of the principal.

options.text: I added earlier interest to the base before calculating the next year
options.feedback: That describes compounding. This question specifies simple interest, so use the original principal each year.

options.text: I used the original principal but chose the wrong description
options.feedback: Then the selected description does not establish compounding. We can check the duration next.

options.text: I am not sure or used another method
options.feedback: The cause remains unknown. Use the original principal for this simple-interest model.

confirm_rate.prompt: How did you use the number {rate}?

options.text: I used it as a fixed peso amount
options.feedback: That supports a percent-unit interpretation in this attempt. The amount changes with the principal; {rate}% means {rate}/100 of it per year.

options.text: I intended a fraction of the principal
options.feedback: Then we should not label the method from the selected description alone. Check the duration next.

options.text: I do not remember or used another method
options.feedback: We do not have enough evidence for a cause. A percent reminder may help.

time.prompt: Which duration matches the question, using years to match the annual rate?

options.text: {duration}
options.feedback: Use that duration with the annual charge.

options.text: {wrong_duration}
options.feedback: Which interpretation led to that duration?

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: The rate is per year. Extra months are divided by 12, not written as decimal digits after the whole years.

confirm_time.prompt: Which describes how you handled the time?

options.text: I wrote the month count directly after the decimal point
options.feedback: Months are twelfths of a year. Six months is 6/12 = one half, not six tenths.

options.text: I calculated only one year and did not include the full duration
options.feedback: That may be an unfinished time step. Include every stated year and any extra months.

options.text: Another method, a mistaken selection, or I do not remember
options.feedback: The reason remains unknown. Match the duration to the annual rate.

time_help.text: A year has 12 months. Six months is half a year. For a whole-year duration, keep all the stated years.

method.prompt: Once the interest for one year is known, how do you find the interest for the whole duration?

options.text: Multiply the annual interest by the duration in years
options.feedback: Yes. Keep that interest result separate from the original loan.

options.text: Add the principal to the annual interest
options.feedback: That gives a different quantity and may also leave out years. The target here is interest alone for the full duration.

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: Simple interest uses the same annual charge for equal years. Count all years and the stated fraction of a year.

hint_1.text: Find 1% of the principal by dividing by 100; multiply by the annual rate numeral. This gives one year’s interest.

hint_2.text: Multiply that annual interest by the full years. For six extra months, add half of one year’s interest.

options.text: The combined fund for both named recipients
options.feedback: Yes. The ratio describes how to split that whole fund.

options.text: Only the second recipient’s share
options.feedback: Which meaning did you give that amount when solving?

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: The wording says the amount is shared or divided. It names the whole fund before the shares are found.

options.text: I treated the given amount as one recipient’s share
options.feedback: That supports a whole-versus-share interpretation in this attempt. Here the amount is both shares combined.

options.text: I knew it was the whole but selected the other description
options.feedback: Then the selection does not establish that misconception. We can check ratio order next.

options.text: I do not remember or used another method
options.feedback: The cause remains unknown. Keep the full fund separate from either share.

order.prompt: In {first_parts}:{second_parts}, which number belongs to the second named recipient?

options.text: {second_parts} parts
options.feedback: Yes. Keep that recipient attached to those parts.

options.text: {first_parts} parts
options.feedback: Did you reverse the recipient order, or was that a mistaken selection?

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: Match the first recipient to the first ratio number and the second recipient to the second number.

options.text: I assigned the first ratio number to the second recipient
options.feedback: That supports an order mix-up here. Ratio order follows recipient order in the wording.

options.text: I intended the second ratio number but selected the first
options.feedback: Then do not infer an order misconception. Check the total number of parts next.

options.text: I used another method or cannot explain yet
options.feedback: We do not know the cause. Label each recipient before counting all parts.

denominator.prompt: How many equal parts does the entire fund contain?

options.text: {sum_parts} parts: {first_parts} + {second_parts}
options.feedback: Yes. One part is the whole fund divided by all those equal parts.

options.text: Only {second_parts} parts
options.feedback: Which rule did you use to divide the whole fund?

options.text: Two equal parts because there are two recipients
options.feedback: Two recipients do not necessarily get equal shares. The ratio counts how many equal-sized units each receives.

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: Count all the ratio parts, not only the parts for the recipient being asked about.

options.text: I divided the whole fund by the requested recipient’s ratio number
options.feedback: That supports a denominator mix-up. To find one equal part, divide by the sum of both ratio numbers.

options.text: I used the sum but chose the wrong description
options.feedback: Then we should not label your denominator from that selection. Check what one part means.

options.text: I cannot remember, guessed, or used another method
options.feedback: The cause remains unknown. We can rebuild the equal-part interpretation.

one_part.prompt: After dividing {total} by {sum_parts}, what have you found?

options.text: The value of one equal ratio part
options.feedback: Yes. The requested recipient receives several such parts.

options.text: The requested recipient’s complete share
options.feedback: Did you stop at one part because you thought that was the whole requested share?

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: That division finds one equal-sized unit. Multiply it by the requested recipient’s number of units.

confirm_unit.prompt: Which best describes why you stopped there?

options.text: I thought one part was the recipient’s entire share
options.feedback: That supports a part-versus-share mix-up in this attempt. The requested recipient gets {second_parts} of those equal parts.

options.text: I knew I still had to multiply but did not finish
options.feedback: That may be incomplete work rather than a conceptual mistake. Include the requested number of parts.

options.text: I do not know or selected the description by mistake
options.feedback: No specific cause is established. Keep one part separate from the full share.

target.prompt: Which final quantity should you report?

options.text: The second named recipient’s share
options.feedback: Yes. Use {second_parts} parts, then check both shares add to {total}.

options.text: The first named recipient’s share
options.feedback: That is a different share. Reread whose amount is requested before multiplying.

options.text: I am not sure
options.feedback: The question asks for the second named recipient. Keep that name beside {second_parts} parts.

hint_1.text: Add the two ratio numbers. That sum counts all the equal parts in the combined fund.

hint_2.text: Divide the total fund by all parts, then multiply one part by the requested recipient’s parts.
